narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 52% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above an even split, so it should be read as a warning signal rather than a certainty; the model judged failure a bit more likely than success, and that tipped the admission decision against you.

The strongest driver was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile in Year 3, while accepted students averaged near the sixth decile, and this low standing was the factor that most strongly pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your high family income bracket, which worked in your favor and pushed toward passing; although high-income students were a small share of accepted applicants, this factor reduced your predicted risk. Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most influential factor and added a smaller amount of support toward passing, not failure. Your undergraduate GPA and Year 1 standing also gave context, but they were less influential than the top three.

To move forward, request a review of the decision if possible, explain any circumstances behind your third-year ranking, and ask what academic evidence would be considered. Strengthen your record through upper-level coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, seek bar-prep advising, and consider retaking the LSAT only if practice results show a clear gain. Then reapply with updated evidence.
